newsitem.title: UK: Rainfall, exports, weigh on Chicago grains prices.
newsitem.headline: Rainfall, exports, weigh on Chicago grains prices.

text.p: A weekend of soaking for the main soyabean growing areas and some corn-fields in the U.S. put buyers in the Chicago grain market pits on the defensive at the start of the week.
"It opened lower on the weather but there was a lot of buying during the lower opening," said Ron Kucha of Chicago traders O'Connor and Co.

Losses of up to eight cents a bushel were seen when the key November soyabean futures position touched $7.92 while December corn dropped 3-1/2 cents to $3.29 a bushel as the rain was seen as crop-enhancing.

Wheat traders showed concern over the possibilty of increased export competition for the U.S. from Canada and Australia, and news of a 100,000 tonnes wheat sale to Egypt failed to smooth these worries.
December wheat was 5-1/2 cents down at one stage at $4.37 a bushel.
Elsewhere, some buying came into robusta coffee futures in London as industry buyers took advantage of last week's four week lows to supplement inventories.
Also of concern to the coffee market was the possibility of delays in shipments from Colombia caused by the threat to the country's infrastructure from truckers protests and guerilla activity.
At one stage November futures on the London Commodity Exchange was trading $22 stg tonne up at $1,556 a tonne.

A week-long meeting of cocoa producers and consumers which started in London on Monday had no market impact on the first day but during the week it was hoped progress will be made towards balancing world supply and demand by way of production controls.

The copper market was relatively stable after last week's collapse and traders were waiting to see if Tuesday's release of the London Metal Exchange copper warehouse inventory figures would continue last Friday's surprise fall.
If so, the price may rally from Monday's close of $1,927 a tonne for benchmark three months delivery metal.

Gold during London trading eroded previous support around $385.00 an ounce and was headed for next support at $382.00 and then at $380.00, with nothing going for the bulls after the market last week failed to respond to U.S. missile attacks on Iraq or the inflatioary implications of strong U.S. jobs data
